topic: Hook: a building that feels its cracks
narration: There is a building in the Philippines that can feel its own cracks. Not metaphorically. Literally.
evidence: Animated cracks spreading across a dark wall, then a city building under the on-screen question 'IS THIS BUILDING STILL SAFE?'
note: Film is animation for 0-96s; this is the film's literal crack/building opening.

topic: Hook: the block inside the walls
narration: Somewhere inside its walls sits a small concrete block — the kind builders use by the thousands, and nobody ever looks at twice — and that block is quietly keeping watch over the whole structure. It knows when the concrete around it is under strain.
evidence: Building interior, white Sentinel module pulsing inside a wall context, building with glowing core, resistance gauge/graph, block transmitting from inside a frame, engineer monitoring in a corridor
note: All animated sequences; module pulse + transmission shots carry the 'quietly keeping watch' clause.

topic: Hook: the block senses strain and reports
narration: It knows when something inside begins to break. And it can report what it feels, without a single person touching the wall. Here is the strange part. This block is not a supercomputer. It is not covered in electronics.
evidence: Crack-growth progression diagram (block to cracked block to failing building), cracked sensor cube under load, building 'speaking' before failure, real resistance-vs-time graph jumping at 'Crack!' beside the hammer test
note: Final segment is real test footage; the rest is the film's animation of internal breakage and reporting.

topic: Hook: not electronics — ordinary material, one hidden difference
narration: It is made of almost the same material as every ordinary block on the building site — with one hidden difference that changes everything. So, three questions. How can concrete — the most ordinary, silent material in construction — feel anything at all?
evidence: Concrete-damage callout on a building, engineer with ordinary wall-mounted external sensors, inventor avatar holding the plain dark block, block transforming with graphene/carbon-fibre callouts, cracked cube close-up, electrical-flow diagram
note: The 49.1-53.0 segment is the film's literal 'concrete + conductive filler = self-sensing concrete' reveal.

topic: After a quake: is this building sound? — for thousands of buildings
narration: Before anyone can safely go back inside, engineers have to answer one question, for thousands of buildings at once: is this structure still sound — or is it damaged in a place nobody can see? Because concrete hides its wounds.

topic: Walls hide cracks; families sleep outside
narration: A wall can look perfectly straight while the material inside it is cracked. And until somebody proves a building is safe, families sleep outside it. For Metro Manila, the scenario engineers plan for is a magnitude 7.2 earthquake.

topic: The old way: eyes and rebound hammers
narration: So how do engineers check a building today? Mostly the way they have for decades — slowly, and by hand. They walk the structure and look for cracks with their eyes. They strike the concrete with rebound hammers, and study what the numbers suggest.
evidence: GM: inspector walks/pans along bridge concrete holding hammer, hammer pressed to column, to bridge soffit and to a concrete wall; WAB: kneeling inspector hammer-tests a foundation block by hand; GM: hand works through handwritten rebound readings and red-annotates the rebound chart (30 N/mm2 written live).
note: Clause map: walk/look = GM 19.5-22.5 (only walking-along-structure passage in either file; no literal crack-inspection walk exists); by-hand/slow = WAB 14.6-17.6; striking = GM 14.5-17.5, GM 52.5-55.5, GM 503.5-506.3; numbers = GM 162.5-165.3 (readings) + GM 296.9-299.7 (chart, low but continuous pen motion). topic: Old methods: slow, late, and they miss internal cracks
narration: These methods work — but they are slow, they are expensive, they usually happen only after damage is already visible, and they can miss the damage that matters most: the cracks forming inside the concrete, where no eye can reach.
evidence: Damaged/collapsed structures throughout: aerial of a fully collapsed building with folded red roof (448.9-452.9), collapsed housing block (303-307), ruined church rubble pile (388.7-392.7), collapsed ACRIGE Apartelle (87-90.4); closing segment shows Civil Defense responders walking a property line inspecting by eye (957-960.1)

topic: Structural health monitoring exists
narration: There is a more advanced option. It is called structural health monitoring — networks of precision sensors fixed onto a building, to watch it full-time. It exists. It is excellent.

topic: The unquestioned rule: concrete is dead material
narration: Underneath all of this sat one rule that nobody questioned: concrete is dead material. It is the dumb, silent part of a building. Sensors are delicate electronics that you attach to a structure afterwards — the building itself could never be the sensor.

topic: Spacer blocks hold rebar at the right distance
narration: When builders pour a concrete wall or column, the steel bars inside it — the rebar — must be held at exactly the right distance from the surface. The small blocks that do that job are called spacer blocks.
evidence: Rebar rods resting across rows of white cover blocks stamped '25' on the demo slab, three clean wide rows with no hand and no overlays

topic: Spacer blocks: cheap, standard, everywhere, forgotten
narration: They are cheap, they are standard, they are already inside almost every reinforced-concrete building in the Philippines — and once the concrete is poured, nobody ever thinks about them again. Ong makes that forgotten block out of a special material: self-sensing concrete.
evidence: Hand holding and rotating a white cover block close to camera (twice), tape measure stretched across a block (twice), full-screen pile of round cover blocks with tie wires
note: Tape windows chosen to avoid subscribe overlays and the picture-in-picture insets (~218-224, ~244+); pile window sits inside the ~343.5-347.5 full-screen pile shot.

topic: DIAGRAM 1: self-sensing concrete — conductive pathways form
narration: It is ordinary concrete, with one change — tiny conductive materials, including graphene and carbon fiber, are mixed through it, forming microscopic electrical pathways inside the block.
note: Covered by the existing mechanism diagram D1.mp4 (one asset spanning beats 28-32, timeline 419.869-500.976). Ruling in graphics-beats.md.

topic: DIAGRAM 2: electrodes + compact electronic module
narration: Two small electrodes are embedded in the block, and after construction, the block is connected to a compact electronic module.
note: Covered by the existing mechanism diagram D1.mp4 (one asset spanning beats 28-32, timeline 419.869-500.976). Ruling in graphics-beats.md.

topic: DIAGRAM 3: the module measures resistance vs the new-block baseline
narration: The module passes a controlled electrical signal through the concrete, and measures its electrical resistance — comparing it, every time, against the reading taken when the block was new and undamaged. While the concrete is healthy, the pathways carry the signal in a steady pattern.
note: Covered by the existing mechanism diagram D1.mp4 (one asset spanning beats 28-32, timeline 419.869-500.976). Ruling in graphics-beats.md.

topic: DIAGRAM 4: cracking breaks pathways — resistance changes
narration: But when an earthquake strains the structure and the concrete cracks, those pathways are broken and disturbed — and the resistance changes, in a way that can be measured. The damage announces itself as a change in a number.
note: Covered by the existing mechanism diagram D1.mp4 (one asset spanning beats 28-32, timeline 419.869-500.976). Ruling in graphics-beats.md.

topic: DIAGRAM 5: readings travel wirelessly to a dashboard
narration: That reading travels wirelessly to an online dashboard, where engineers can watch the building's condition over time — and after an earthquake, see at a glance which parts of the structure are signalling that they need a closer look.
note: Covered by the existing mechanism diagram D1.mp4 (one asset spanning beats 28-32, timeline 419.869-500.976). Ruling in graphics-beats.md.

topic: First check happens on a screen
